:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Find $q$, if $7a_{1} + qa_{2} = b$ and
$a_{1} = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}, a_{2} = \begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}, b = \begin{bmatrix}32 \\ 17\end{bmatrix}$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $h$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}+h{a}_{2} & =b \\ 3\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+h\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 14 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ h\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 14 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ h\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 4 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $h=2.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $m$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}7{a}_{1}+m{a}_{2} & =b \\ 7\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+m\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -12\end{bmatrix} \\ m\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}-7\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ m\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-15 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $m=-5.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $k$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2} & =b \\ 2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+k\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -7 \\ -12\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -7 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $k=-3.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $j$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}-j{a}_{2} & =b \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-j\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ j\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ j\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $j=2.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $k$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2} & =0 \\ 3\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+k\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the first components, we get 

$$
3k=-6\,⟹\,k=-2.
$$

But then

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\ne \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $k$ such that $3{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2}=0.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $l$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5{a}_{1}+l{a}_{2} & =b \\ 5\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+l\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -15 \\ 25 \\ 16\end{bmatrix} \\ l\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -15 \\ 25 \\ 16\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ l\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 15 \\ -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that 
$l=3.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $k$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2} & =0 \\ 8\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 6 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}+k\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-8\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 6 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}24 \\ -48 \\ 32\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the first components, we get 

$$
-2k=24\,⟹\,k=-12.
$$

But then 

$$
\begin{aligned}-12\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}24 \\ -36 \\ 48\end{bmatrix}\ne \begin{bmatrix}24 \\ -48 \\ 32\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $k$ such that 
 $8{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2}=0.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $m$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5{a}_{1}+m{a}_{2} & =0 \\ 5\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+m\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ m\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ m\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-30 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the first components, we get 

$$
-5m=-30\,⟹\,m=6.
$$

But then

$$
\begin{aligned}6\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-30 \\ 18\end{bmatrix}\ne \begin{bmatrix}-30 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $m$ such that $5{a}_{1}+m{a}_{2}=0.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $q$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}+q{a}_{2} & =b \\ 2\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+q\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}18 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ q\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}18 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\ q\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $q=2.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $t$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}+t{a}_{2} & =0 \\ 2\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ t\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\ t\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-16 \\ -2 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the first components, we get 

$$
-4t=-16\,⟹\,t=4.
$$

But then 

$$
\begin{aligned}4\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}\ne \begin{bmatrix}-16 \\ -2 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $t$ such that 
 $2{a}_{1}+t{a}_{2}=0.$

Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $k$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2} & =b \\ 6\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+k\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 3 \\ -9\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 3 \\ -9\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 3 \\ -9\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -6 \\ 18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $k=-2.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the vectors



$$
\mathbf{c_1}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{c_2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$



If $x_1 \mathbf{c}_1 + x_2\mathbf{c}_2  = \mathbf d,$ then what is $x_1+x_2?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If $x_1 \mathbf{c}_1 + x_2\mathbf{c}_2  = \mathbf d,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=5 \\ -{x}_{1} &=-5 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we obtain $x_1=5,$ which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =5 \\ 4(5)+{x}_{2} & =5 \\ {x}_{2} & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x_1=5$ and $x_2=-15$ into the third equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 3(5)+(-15) & =0 \\ 0 & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is $x_1=5$ and $x_2=-15,$ which means

$$
5 \mathbf{c_1}-15 \mathbf{c_2} = \mathbf{d}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2=5-15=-10.
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Solving for Two Coefficients in a Linear Combination

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the vectors



$$
\mathbf{a_1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{a_2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{a_3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.
$$



If $x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2 + x_3\mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf b,$ then what is $x_1+x_2+x_3?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{b}$ is a linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{a_1}, \,\mathbf{a_2}$ and $\mathbf{a_3}$ with coefficients $x_1,\, x_2$ and $x_3,$ respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3} & =b \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:



$$
M= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{array} \right]
$$



Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $x_3 = 2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_2 = -1,
$$

and substituting $x_3=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x_1+2(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_1 = -3.
$$

So the solution of the system is $x_1=-3, x_2=-1, x_3=2,$ which means

$$
-3 \mathbf{a_1}- \mathbf{a_2} +2 \mathbf{a_3}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2+x_3=-3-1+2=-2.
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider a vector $\mathbf{u}$ which is given in terms of the vectors $\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\mathbf{v_2}$ as follows:

$$
{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}\mathbf{v_1}}+({\color{red}-2}){\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}} = \mathbf{u}
$$

Here, we say that $\mathbf{u}$ is a **linear combination** of the vectors ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v_1}}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}$ with coefficients ${\color{red}3}$ and ${\color{red}-2}$ respectively. 

In general, a linear combination of $n$ vectors $\mathbf{v_1},\mathbf{v_2},\dots,\mathbf{v_n}$ is the *weighted sum*

$$
{\color{red}x_1}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1}+{\color{red}x_2}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2}+\cdots + {\color{red}x_n}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_n} = \mathbf{u},
$$

where ${\color{red}x_1},{\color{red}x_2},\dots,{\color{red}x_n}\in\mathbb{R}.$ We say that $\mathbf{u}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2},\dots,\mathbf{\color{blue}v_n}$ with coefficients (or *weights*) ${\color{red}x_1},{\color{red}x_2},\dots,{\color{red}x_n},$ respectively.

For instance, 


$$
{\color{red}2} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{\large\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1} + {\color{red}0} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{\large\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} + {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{2}} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{\large\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3}
$$


is the linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_3}$ with coefficients ${\color{red}2}, {\color{red}0}, {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{2}},$ respectively.

$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $s=4.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate $\mathbf{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a+2x & =b \\ 2x & =b-a \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}(b-a) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}(\begin{bmatrix}24 \\ -9 \\ 13\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ 2 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\ x & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 1 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving for a Vector in a Linear Combination

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the vectors



$$
\mathbf{c_1}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{c_2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$



If $x_1 \mathbf{c}_1 + x_2\mathbf{c}_2  = \mathbf d,$ then what is $x_1+x_2?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If $x_1 \mathbf{c}_1 + x_2\mathbf{c}_2  = \mathbf d,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=5 \\ -{x}_{1} &=-5 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we obtain $x_1=5,$ which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =5 \\ 4(5)+{x}_{2} & =5 \\ {x}_{2} & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x_1=5$ and $x_2=-15$ into the third equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 3(5)+(-15) & =0 \\ 0 & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is $x_1=5$ and $x_2=-15,$ which means

$$
5 \mathbf{c_1}-15 \mathbf{c_2} = \mathbf{d}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2=5-15=-10.
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving for Two Coefficients in a Linear Combination

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the vectors



$$
\mathbf{a_1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{a_2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{a_3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.
$$



If $x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2 + x_3\mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf b,$ then what is $x_1+x_2+x_3?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{b}$ is a linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{a_1}, \,\mathbf{a_2}$ and $\mathbf{a_3}$ with coefficients $x_1,\, x_2$ and $x_3,$ respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3} & =b \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ -{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:



$$
M= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{array} \right]
$$



Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $x_3 = 2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_2 = -1,
$$

and substituting $x_3=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x_1+2(2) = 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_1 = -3.
$$

So the solution of the system is $x_1=-3, x_2=-1, x_3=2,$ which means

$$
-3 \mathbf{a_1}- \mathbf{a_2} +2 \mathbf{a_3}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
x_1+x_2+x_3=-3-1+2=-2.
$$

First, we apply the addition principle, adding $7$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    		3p-7 &=20\\
		3p-7+7 &=20+7 \\
                3p + 0 &= 27 \\
		3p &=27
	\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
		3p &=27 \\[5pt]
		\dfrac{3p}{3} &=\dfrac{27}{3} \\[5pt]  
		\dfrac{\cancel{3}p}{\cancel{3}} &= 9 \\[5pt]

	\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Solving Linear Equations that Involve Multiplication

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To save time, we will keep the variable on the right-hand side as we solve. First, we apply the addition principle, adding $8$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =5x-8 \\ 2+8 & =5x-8+8 \\ 10 & =5x+0 \\ 10 & =5x\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =5x \\ \frac{10}{5} & =\frac{5x}{5} \\ 2 & =\frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} \\ 2 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2=x,$ we conclude that the solution is $x=2.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
After converting the equation to a more familiar form, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $7$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
               7-\dfrac{p}{3} &=9 \\
    		-\dfrac{p}{3}+7 &=9\\
		-\dfrac{p}{3}+7-7 &= 9-7 \\
		-\dfrac{p}{3}+0 &= 2 \\
		-\dfrac{p}{3} &=2
	\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle. We multiply by $-1$ to get rid of the negative sign, and again by $3$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
               -\dfrac{p}{3} &=2 \\
              (-1) \cdot \left( -\dfrac{p}{3} \right) &=(-1) \cdot 2 \\
		\dfrac{p}{3} &=-2 \\
		\cancel{3} \cdot \dfrac{p}{\cancel{3}} &=3 \cdot (-2) \\
		p &=-6
	\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Solving Linear Equations that Involve Division

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we apply the addition principle, adding $\dfrac{1}{2}$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    		-\dfrac{z}{3}-\dfrac 1 2 &=\dfrac 7 2\\[5pt]
		-\dfrac{z}{3} - \dfrac 1 2+\dfrac 1 2 &= \dfrac 7 2+\dfrac 1 2 \\[5pt]
-\dfrac{z}{3} + 0 &= \dfrac 7 2+\dfrac 1 2 \\[5pt]
		-\dfrac{z}{3} &=\dfrac 8 2 \\[5pt]
		-\dfrac{z}{3} &=4
	\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle. We multiply by $-1$ to get rid of the negative sign, and again by $3$ to get rid of the fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\dfrac{z}{3} &=4 \\
(-1) \cdot \left( -\dfrac{z}{3} \right) &= (-1) \cdot 4 \\[5pt]
		\dfrac{z}{3} &=-4 \\[5pt]
		\cancel{3} \cdot \dfrac{z}{\cancel{3}} &= 3 \cdot (-4) \\[5pt]   
		z &=-12
	\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Let be ![](images/87/870f39e6853ca1dc2013d9b82beb35e1533a3d4b5f2318cf607f1f19efdeb0d7.svg) and ![](images/9f/9f51885fedc5cf606a4e2c48663c5e85df144fe004adf7795677a3a4dc37218a.svg) If $\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{b}=0,$ find the value of $x.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Starting from the equation $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}=0,$ we compute the dot product in terms of $x$ and then solve for $x$ in the resulting equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 10\cdot x+x\cdot x+0\cdot 8+5\cdot 5 & =0 \\ 10x+{x}^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+10x+25 & =0 \\ (x+5)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $x=-5.$
